Points, lines and planes: A point names an exact location and has no size. A line extends forever in both directions and is determined by any two of its points. A plane is a flat surface that extends forever in all directions and is determined by three points that are not on one line. Points on one line are collinear; points in one plane are coplanar. A segment is the part of a line between two endpoints, and a ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. Two different lines meet in at most one point, and two different planes that meet, meet in a line.
Segments, angles and measurement: The length of a segment is found with a ruler, and segments with the same length are congruent. The midpoint splits a segment into two congruent parts. Segment Addition Postulate: if B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC. An angle is formed by two rays with a common vertex and is measured in degrees: acute is less than 90, right is exactly 90, obtuse is between 90 and 180 and straight is 180. An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal angles. Angle Addition Postulate: if ray OB is inside angle AOC, then angle AOB + angle BOC = angle AOC. Complementary angles add to 90 and supplementary angles add to 180. Vertical angles are equal.
Distance and midpoint formulas: For points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): the distance is d = square root of ((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2), which comes from the Pythagorean theorem, and the midpoint is M = ((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2). Example: A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) give distance square root of (36 + 64) = 10 and midpoint (4, 6). To find a missing endpoint, double the midpoint coordinates and subtract the known endpoint coordinates.
Reflections, translations and rotations: Reflections, translations and rotations are rigid motions: they keep distances and angle measures, so the image is congruent to the original. A translation slides every point the same distance in the same direction, (x, y) becomes (x + a, y + b). A reflection flips the figure across a line: over the x-axis (x, y) becomes (x, -y), over the y-axis (-x, y), over the line y = x (y, x). A rotation turns the figure about a point: 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin gives (-y, x), 180 degrees gives (-x, -y) and 270 degrees counterclockwise gives (y, -x).
Dilations and symmetry: A dilation has a center and a scale factor k. Every distance from the center is multiplied by k. About the origin, (x, y) becomes (kx, ky). If k is greater than 1 the figure gets bigger (an enlargement), if k is between 0 and 1 it gets smaller (a reduction). Angles stay the same, lengths are multiplied by k and areas by k squared. The image is similar to the original, not congruent unless k = 1.
